name: Wendy Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me your public view and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Hartwell Farm, which is six thousand free-range hens, a flock of about two hundred ewes and some barley. Rob Hartwell owns it; he's 45 and runs it like a small business. I start at seven, walk the hen houses, check the drinkers, then I'm in the packing room grading and boxing eggs till lunch. Afternoons it's sheep, or cleaning, or whatever Rob needs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I had my own hair salon for twenty-five years, Wendy's on Station Road. At 55 I'd had enough of the chemicals and standing on tiles, so I sold it, paid off the mortgage and asked Rob for a job, because he was a client. Three years in, I'm still the newest, and Rob still has to tell me when a hen looks off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the packing room radio and the routine, and I love the sheep, which surprised me. What wears me out is the dust in the hen houses and the early winters. I use AI every day, honestly; I ask it about hen diseases, I used it to build Rob a spreadsheet for egg sizes, and my husband Ken uses it in his garage to read fault codes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, it was useful but it wasn't magic, which is what I always thought. At Hartwell I'd say the hens are happy either way. Online I'd post a picture of an egg and say 'still made by hand'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing much for me. My work's secure, the mortgage is paid, Ken's garage is busy, and we've five months saved. I'd be a bit sorry, because I like the tools, but it doesn't change my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Hartwell and keep using AI for the little things. I'd offer Rob to set up the egg orders for the farm shops on an AI tool, because he still does them on paper. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable, really. Selling my hair salon was the scariest thing I've done, and after that a hen house holds no fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Rob still does the orders on paper. Why hasn't he changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rob's busy, and he says paper doesn't crash. I'd show him once on my phone and he'd come round. He trusts me with that sort of thing more than with the hens, funnily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the next few years that worries you even in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knees, a bit, and the dust in the hen houses. And whether the twins, Mia and Leo, settle down. But money-wise, no, we're fine.

say: AI was **useful but not magic**, which is what I always thought.
Online I'd post an egg photo saying **still made by hand**.
think: My work's **secure**: mortgage paid, Ken's garage busy, five months saved.
I'd be **a bit sorry**, because I enjoy the tools.
do: Keep working the **packing room** and hen houses at Hartwell.
Set up the **farm shop orders** on an AI tool so Rob stops using paper.
feel: **Calm** and comfortable, with only knees and dust as small worries.
S0.quote: Selling my hair salon was the scariest thing I've done, and after that a hen house holds no fear.
fieldNote: A paid-off **mortgage** and Ken's busy garage make her feel genuinely secure.
Though junior on the farm, she is Rob's **go-to for tech**.
Selling her **salon** gave her confidence in big changes.

steps.text: Keep grading and packing eggs at Hartwell
Move Rob's farm-shop egg orders from paper to an AI tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to get rid of the boring bits, and anyone who's sensible will learn it now. At Hartwell I'd tell Rob to let the AI do the orders and the bookkeeping. Online I'd share tips for people my age, because we're not as useless as they think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a good spot. The thinking side of the farm, orders and records and planning, goes to AI, and I'm the one who already uses it. The hen houses and packing are hands-on, so robots come slowly, and I'd be the one who knows how to work with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd set up the AI for Rob's orders, records and feed planning, and show him how to check it. I'd look at the egg-collecting robots that roll round the hen house floor and price one for him. And I'd keep doing my normal job while all that beds in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. It feels like when I brought online booking into the salon and the old girls moaned, then loved it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would bringing in an egg-collecting robot cost anyone their job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might cut some of my floor-egg collecting, which I hate anyway. Rob has two part-timers, Gail and Tom, and I'd make sure he moved them onto the sheep, not out the door. I'd say that to Rob's face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ken's garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ken's garage gets busier, if anything. AI tells my husband Ken what's wrong with a car, but somebody still has to lie on a cold floor and fix it.

say: It's a chance to **drop the boring bits**, and sensible people learn it now.
I'd share **tips** for people my age, who aren't as useless as people think.
think: I'm in a **good spot**, since the farm's thinking work goes to AI and I already use it.
Hen house work is **hands-on**, so robots come slowly and I'll know how to work with them.
do: Set up AI this winter for Rob's **orders, records** and feed planning.
Price an **egg-collecting robot** for the hen house floor.
Make sure Rob moves **Gail and Tom** onto the sheep, not out.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**, like bringing online booking into the salon.
S1.quote: AI tells my husband Ken what's wrong with a car, but somebody still has to lie on a cold floor and fix it.
fieldNote: She sees Steady Disruption as hitting the **owner's desk work**, which she can help with.
She would push **automation** but defend part-timers' jobs.
**Ken's garage** feels like a hands-on safe place to her.

steps.text: Set up AI for Rob's orders, records and feed planning
Price an egg-collecting floor robot for the hen houses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough and people need to move fast. At Hartwell I'd tell Rob we should be first, not last. Online I'd be honest that it scares me a bit, even though I like the stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 the planning and orders are AI, fine. By 2031 a robot can pack eggs and walk the hen houses, and I'm 63. I'd planned to stop at 64, so it's a year early, unless I'm the one who looks after the robots, which I think I could be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd do the short course on farm robots at the college, so I'm the obvious person to run them. I'd put four thousand of our savings into a pension top-up, because our income will drop sooner than we planned. And I'd help Rob choose the egg-packing robot, so it's one I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. I think my own job is fine because Rob needs someone who isn't scared of the machines. But it's on my mind every day, and I'd lie awake for Gail and Tom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound confident. What if Rob decides he doesn't need you either?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I stop a year early and we live on Ken's garage and the pension. Running the hair salon taught me that you can't stop the change, but you can be the one holding the scissors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ken in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ken is 62 and he'd say robots can't fix a 2009 diesel van. Maybe not, but the new cars won't need him. He's talking about closing at 65 anyway.

say: It'll be **rough**, and people need to move fast.
I'd admit online that it **scares me** a bit, even though I like the tools.
think: By **2031** a robot can pack eggs and walk the hen houses, and I'm 63.
I could be **the one** who looks after the robots, so I might keep my job.
do: Do the college's **farm robots course** straight away.
Put **four thousand** of savings into a pension top-up.
Help Rob choose an **egg-packing robot** that I can work with.
feel: **Uneasy** but fairly confident about my own job.
**Worried** for the part-timers Gail and Tom.
S2.quote: Running the hair salon taught me that you can't stop the change, but you can be the one holding the scissors.
fieldNote: She reasons that **owners need** someone unafraid of machines, which protects her.
Losing work at 63 would cost only **one year** of her plan.
Her worry turns outward to the **part-timers** rather than herself.

steps.text: Take the college's short course on farm robots
Put 4,000 of savings into a pension top-up
Help Rob choose an egg-packing robot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if we're smart. At Hartwell I'd say let's plan it properly. Online I'd write about how the salon changed with online bookings, because it's the same story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's easier for me. AGI in 2031, robots in 2034 when I'm 66, so I'd have stopped. I could help bring in the robots and then hand over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Rob put a five-year plan together: AI for orders now, egg-packing robot about 2033. I'd do the robot course in my own time. And I'd put a couple of thousand into an index fund, since we have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested. It's the version where I get to help and then leave on a high.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would leaving on a high look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to train Gail on the egg-packing robot first. On my last day I'd walk out of the Hartwell packing room with a box of eggs and a bunch of flowers. That would be a nice end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that bothers you in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The twins. Mia does marketing and Leo does insurance claims, both desk jobs. I'd be telling them to plan now, every Sunday lunch.

say: **Five years** is enough if we're smart about it.
I'd write online about how the **salon** changed with online bookings.
think: Robots in **2034** come when I'm 66, after I've stopped.
I could **help bring in** the robots and then hand over.
do: Help Rob write a **five-year plan**: AI orders now, egg robot around 2033.
Put a couple of thousand into an **index fund**.
feel: **Calm** and interested, picturing leaving on a high.
S3.quote: On my last day I'd walk out of the Hartwell packing room with a box of eggs and a bunch of flowers.
fieldNote: **Five years** lets her help with the change and retire on schedule.
Her concern shifts to the **twins' desk jobs**.
She pictures a **graceful handover** to Gail.

steps.text: Help Rob write a five-year plan for an egg-packing robot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, and anyone who's caught out wasn't paying attention. At Hartwell I'd say we've got time to do it nicely. Online I'd probably not bother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't touch my job at all. I'll be gone well before 2039. It's about the twins and the grandchildren now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Hartwell and keep using the AI for the farm side. I'd sit the twins down and help them think about retraining over the decade, and I'd offer to help with course fees. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relaxed, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mia and Leo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my twins, Mia and Leo, to learn one thing a robot can't do yet and one thing it can, and be good at both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you help pay for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. We've no mortgage and Ken's garage pays well, so a few hundred towards a course each is fine.

At Hartwell we'd have **time to do it** nicely.
think: My job is **untouched**, as I'll be gone well before 2039.
It's about the **twins** and grandchildren now.
do: Carry on at **Hartwell** and keep using AI for the farm side.
Offer the twins a **few hundred each** towards retraining courses.
S4.quote: I'd tell my twins, Mia and Leo, to learn one thing a robot can't do yet and one thing it can, and be good at both.
fieldNote: A decade's warning removes all **personal risk** for her.
She'd turn her energy to the **twins' retraining**.
Money **comfort** comes from the paid mortgage and Ken's garage.

steps.text: Carry on packing eggs and using AI at Hartwell

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, mostly for Gail and Tom and the twins, and a little for me. What would help is free short courses on the robots for people already on farms, so the owners train us rather than replace us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people my age what they've already lived through. I went from perm rollers to online booking in one career, so a robot egg packer doesn't frighten me.

headlineQuote: I went from perm rollers to online booking in one career, so a robot egg packer doesn't frighten me.
portrait: Wendy is a **58-year-old** egg packer at Hartwell Farm who sold her hair salon of twenty-five years.
She uses **AI daily** and is Rob's go-to for tech, though junior with the hens.
With a **paid-off mortgage** and Ken's busy garage, she feels secure and stays calm in most scenarios.
Only **AGI by 2028** makes her uneasy, and even then she expects to run the robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mainly for the part-timers and her **twins**.
whatWouldHelp: **Free short courses** on farm robots, so owners train staff rather than replace them.
